correction.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman precisely contrasts Matthew’s conspicuously detached third-person self-description with Acts’ anonymous first-person narration, directly challenging both proposed internal identifications through readily intelligible and textually anchored observations. Principal limitation: The argument establishes underdetermination more securely than competing authorship, because third-person narration can coexist with mediated self-reference and first-person participation may acquire cumulative significance alongside independent external testimony. Live burden: Licona must explain why these formally nonidentifying narrative features, separately or cumulatively, uniquely support Matthew and Luke rather than merely remaining compatible with inherited attribution traditions. Locked score: At 90, this is a very strong, exceptionally responsive central reply whose disciplined negative scope, stable terminology, and proportionate probabilistic force outweigh its limited treatment of cumulative evidence.
